Akureyri is a major cruise port and one of Iceland's oldest towns, located approx 240 km (150 mi) northeast of the country's capital city Reykjavik. Akureyri features picturesque historic houses below snowcapped peaks, several museums and botanical gardens. It is the biggest settlement outside southwest of Iceland, and one of country's largest cities. "Akureyri" means "Meadow Sandspit" in Icelandic.

You can visit the villages Hauganes and Dalvik (located at the lower end of Eyjafjordur, along fjord's shore) or the islands Grimsey and Hrisey. Go inland to explore Lake Myvatn - famous bird sanctuary, with one of world's largest breeding duck colonies. En-route to Lake Myvatn, you can see amazing lava formations, craters and Grotagja fissure (former public bath). At the Godafoss Waterfall, the Nordic gods Thor and Odin watch over Iceland. Myvatn is a lush area with abundant bird and fish life. Another must-see is Krafla area and its huge lava fields.

In 2017, the cruise port handled a total of 124 ship calls. This number grew to 138 in 2018 (around 130,000 passengers). Summer cruising season's most popular month is July. Most of the visiting vessels are on Iceland circumnavigation itineraries. In 2017 was inaugurated a tree-planting program, by which around 2000 trees are planted per cruise season.

Also from Akureyri cruise port, tourists access one of Iceland's best-known natural attractions - Hverir (Lake Myvatn, east of Mount Namafjall). Hverir (aka Hverarond) is a barren area with high-temperature geothermal activity (hot springs).

In February 2018, Port Akureyri announced an investment of EUR 5 million in building a new cruise pier (completed in 2019). The new pier has length 130 m (427 ft) and depth 9 m (20 ft). Season 2018's main highlight was the 170,000-ton cruise liner MSC Meraviglia (max passenger capacity 5386) that was scheduled for anchoring on May 24 (port stay 8 am - 7 pm). This was the largest ever ship visiting Port Akureyri. The call was part of 21-day roundtrip itinerary from homeport Hamburg Germany to ports in Norway and Iceland.

Akureyri cruise terminal

In 2017, Port Akureyri's services were upgraded with a modern, high-power tugboat. The cruise berth expansion project to lengthen port's main docking pier by 100 m (328 ft) to total 270 m (886 m) was started in 2018 and completed in 2019. The facility allows berthing of cruise vessels with GT tonnage under 10,000 tons.

Located just 100 m (330 ft) from downtown, another pier will be rebuilt/expanded in 2020 and ready for season 2021.

At a Glance

Independent sightseeing: Easy. Akureyri is one of Iceland's most convenient cruise ports for exploring on foot. Most cruise ships berth close to the compact town center, generally within about a 5-10 minute walk. The main sights, waterfront, shops, cafés, Akureyri Church and Botanical Garden can all be combined without needing a tour.

For passengers who want to see North Iceland's major natural attractions, Goðafoss is manageable independently with advance transport planning, while a longer Lake Mývatn itinerary is usually better suited to an organized excursion because of the distances and limited port-call time.

Getting from the Cruise Port

Akureyri has several cruise berths. Larger ships commonly use Tangabryggja and Oddeyrarbryggja, while smaller vessels can use Torfunefsbryggja. The port also has anchorage and tender facilities, so the exact arrival arrangement depends on the ship and berth allocation.

Most docked passengers can simply walk into central Akureyri. Hof Cultural and Conference Centre, which contains the tourist information office, is close to the harbor and is a useful orientation point. Ráðhústorg square and the main central streets are only a few minutes farther.

  • Walking: Best option for central sightseeing.
  • Local buses: Akureyri's municipal buses are free and can be useful for reaching the Botanical Garden, museums and residential areas farther from the waterfront.
  • Taxis: Useful for attractions outside town and for passengers with limited mobility.
  • Regional buses: Depart near Hof and can reach places including Goðafoss, but services and capacity are limited, making them less flexible for cruise passengers.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Explore Central Akureyri on Foot

Allow about 2-4 hours. This is the simplest independent option. Walk from the harbor past Hof to the center, explore Hafnarstræti and Ráðhústorg, then climb to Akureyri Church. Continue through the Art Street area and, if time permits, the Botanical Garden.

The center itself is compact, but Akureyri rises steeply away from the waterfront. The climb to the church and higher streets can be tiring for passengers with limited mobility.

Visit the Botanical Garden and Old Town

Allow about 3-4 hours including walking. The Akureyri Botanical Garden is a practical extension of a town walk and is accessible year-round. From there, continue south toward the older part of Akureyri, where historic wooden houses, Nonni's House and Akureyri Museum are located.

The Old Town museums are roughly a 20-30 minute walk from the center. A free local bus can reduce the walking if necessary.

Goðafoss Waterfall

Allow about 2.5-3.5 hours. Goðafoss is approximately 35 km (21.7 mi) from Akureyri and normally takes around 35-45 minutes each way by road. It is one of the easiest major North Iceland attractions to fit into a cruise call.

Options include cruise-oriented transfers, excursions, taxi or rental car. Regional bus Route 79 also stops near Goðafoss, but capacity is limited and schedules should be checked carefully before relying on it for a ship day. An organized transfer is safer when the port call is short.

Lake Mývatn and Volcanic Landscapes

Allow about 5-7 hours. The Lake Mývatn area is approximately 85 km (52.8 mi) from Akureyri, about an hour's drive before sightseeing stops are added. Typical itineraries combine Goðafoss with volcanic and geothermal locations such as Skútustaðagígar, Dimmuborgir and the Hverir geothermal area.

Organized excursion recommended. The attractions are spread over a wide area and much of the day is spent driving. Independent rental-car touring is possible during a sufficiently long port call, but it requires careful route planning and a substantial return margin.

Whale Watching in Eyjafjörður

Allow about 3-4 hours. Whale-watching boats operate from the waterfront near Hof, making this one of the most convenient wildlife activities for cruise passengers. Humpback whales are among the species regularly encountered in Eyjafjörður, although wildlife sightings can never be guaranteed.

This can be booked independently because departures are close to the cruise area, but passengers should choose a sailing that returns comfortably before all-aboard time.

Forest Lagoon

Allow about 2.5-3.5 hours. Forest Lagoon is on the opposite side of the fjord, a short drive from central Akureyri. Walking from the center takes roughly 40 minutes and is less attractive when port time is limited.

A complimentary seasonal shuttle operates on selected dates between the harbor area and the lagoon, with additional city-center service at certain times. Pre-book the lagoon and verify the shuttle schedule for the specific cruise date rather than assuming that harbor transfers operate every day.

Self-Guided Walking Tours

Central Akureyri and Waterfront — Easy

Distance: approximately 2-2.5 km (1.2-1.6 mi)
Pure walking time: about 30-40 minutes
Recommended total time: 1.5-2.5 hours
Difficulty: Easy, mostly level with only minor gradients.

  1. Cruise berth: Walk toward the central waterfront.
  2. Hof Cultural and Conference Centre: Stop for tourist information, maps and orientation.
  3. Ráðhústorg: Enter the compact center and pedestrian shopping area.
  4. Hafnarstræti: Walk the main central street past cafés, shops and traditional buildings.
  5. Oddeyri waterfront: Follow part of the coastal area for views across Eyjafjörður.
  6. Return to the harbor: Follow the waterfront back toward the ship.

This route is suitable for a short call, poor weather or passengers who do not want the steeper climbs found above the town center.

Church, Botanical Garden and Old Town — Moderate

Distance: approximately 4.5-5 km (2.8-3.1 mi)
Pure walking time: about 60-75 minutes
Recommended total time: 3-4 hours with stops
Difficulty: Moderate. Paved streets and paths, but with a noticeable uphill section from the center.

  1. Cruise berth and Hof: Walk into the center via the waterfront.
  2. Ráðhústorg and Hafnarstræti: Explore the main town-center streets.
  3. Akureyri Church: Climb from the center for views over the town and fjord.
  4. Art Street: Continue through Kaupvangsstræti past the Akureyri Art Museum and surrounding cultural buildings.
  5. Akureyri Botanical Garden: Walk through the landscaped garden before continuing south.
  6. Old Town: Follow the historic streets toward Nonni's House and Akureyri Museum.
  7. Return: Walk north along Aðalstræti and Hafnarstræti toward the center, then continue to the cruise berth.

If the Old Town extension becomes too long, turn back from the Botanical Garden. Free city buses can also shorten the return journey.

Practical Tips

  • Akureyri is unusually easy to explore without a cruise-line excursion; do not feel obliged to book transport simply to see the town.
  • Expect hills. The waterfront and central shopping streets are relatively easy, but the church, Botanical Garden and upper neighborhoods require climbing.
  • Icelandic weather can change quickly even in summer. Carry a waterproof outer layer and suitable walking shoes.
  • For Goðafoss or Lake Mývatn, check road and weather conditions before leaving Akureyri, particularly outside the main summer season.
  • Do not build a long independent itinerary around a single regional bus connection. Services are limited compared with city transport.
  • For distant excursions, leave a substantial return margin. Traffic, weather, road conditions, tour delays and tender operations can all reduce usable time ashore.
